title: Check If a String Can Break Another String
statement:
You get two strings `s1` and `s2` with the same length `n`. A string `x` is said to *break* a string `y` of equal length when, at every index `i` from `0` to `n - 1`, the letter `x[i]` equals `y[i]` or comes after it in the alphabet.

You may reorder the letters of each string freely. Return `true` if some reordering of `s1` breaks some reordering of `s2`, or some reordering of `s2` breaks some reordering of `s1`. Otherwise return `false`.
constraints: s1 and s2 contain only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every pair of reorderings is hopeless. The useful observation is that if any reordering of `s1` can break `s2`, then sorting both strings also works: pairing the smallest letter of one with the smallest of the other, the second smallest with the second smallest, and so on, is the best possible matching. So sort both strings and compare them position by position, in both directions at once.

## Approach

1. Sort the letters of `s1` into `sorted1` and those of `s2` into `sorted2`.
2. Assume both directions can work: `firstBreaks` (`s1` breaks `s2`) and `secondBreaks` (`s2` breaks `s1`) start as `true`.
3. Walk the positions. A smaller letter in `sorted1` rules out `firstBreaks`; a larger letter rules out `secondBreaks`.
4. Return `true` if either flag survives.

## Example 1, step by step

`sorted1 = [a, b, c]` and `sorted2 = [a, x, y]`. At `i = 0` both are `a`, so nothing changes. At `i = 1`, `b < x`, so `firstBreaks` becomes `false`. At `i = 2`, `c < y` again. `secondBreaks` never fails, so `s2` can break `s1` and the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the two sorts; the scan is O(n). Counting sort over 26 letters would make it O(n).
- Space: O(n) for the sorted letter arrays.

## Pitfalls

- Check both directions; the stronger string may be either `s1` or `s2`.
- Equal letters do not rule out either direction, so use strict `<` and `>`.
- Strings in JavaScript are immutable, so split into an array before sorting.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sorted1`, `sorted2` | the letters of `s1` and `s2` in alphabetical order |
| `firstBreaks` | still possible that `s1` breaks `s2` |
| `secondBreaks` | still possible that `s2` breaks `s1` |
| `i` | the position being compared |

narration.2: Sort the letters of s1 so the smallest letters line up first.
narration.3: Sort s2 the same way; sorted order is the best pairing for both directions.
narration.4: Assume for now that s1 can break s2.
narration.5: Assume as well that s2 can break s1.
narration.7: Compare the two sorted strings one position at a time.
narration.8: A smaller letter in s1 here means s1 cannot break s2.
narration.11: A larger letter in s1 here means s2 cannot break s1.
narration.15: If either direction survived every position, one string breaks the other.
